section.heading: 12.2. Vectors
section.paragraph: The term vector is used in mathematics and the sciences to indicate a quantity that has both magnitude and direction. For instance, to describe the velocity of a moving object, we must specify both the speed of the object and the direction of travel. Other examples of vectors include force, displacement, and acceleration.
section.heading: Geometric Description of Vectors
section.paragraph: A vector is often represented by an arrow or a directed line segment. The length of the arrow represents the magnitude of the vector and the arrow points in the direction of the vector. We denote a vector by printing a letter in boldface $$\left( \mathbf{v} \right)$$ or by putting an arrow above the letter $$(\overset{\rightarrow}{v})$$ .

For instance, suppose a particle moves along a line segment from point $$A$$ to point $$B$$ . The corresponding displacement vector $$\mathbf{v}$$ , shown in Figure 1, has initial point $$A$$ (the tail) and terminal point $$B$$ (the tip) and we indicate this by writing $$\mathbf{v} = \overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{AB}}$$ . Notice that the vector $$\mathbf{u} = \overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{CD}}$$ has the same length and the same direction as $$\mathbf{v}$$ even though it is in a different position. We say that $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ are equivalent (or equal) and we write $$\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{v}$$ . The zero vector, denoted by $$0$$ , has length $$0$$ . It is the only vector with no specific direction.

The second vector, labeled vector u, begins from C, is located up and to the right of A, runs parallel to vector v, has the same length as vector v, and ends at D.

section.paragraph: We will often find it useful to combine vectors. For example, suppose a particle moves from $$A$$ to $$B$$ with displacement vector $$\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{AB}}$$ , and then the particle changes direction and moves from $$B$$ to $$C$$ , with displacement vector $$\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{BC}}$$ , as shown in Figure 2. The combined effect of these displacements is that the particle has moved from $$A$$ to $$C$$ . The resulting displacement vector $$\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{AC}}$$ is called the sum of $$\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{AB}}$$ and $$\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{BC}}$$ and we write
$$\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{AC}} = \overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{AB}} + \overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{BC}}$$

section.paragraph: In general, if we start with vectors $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ , we first place $$\mathbf{v}$$ so that its tail coincides with the tip of $$\mathbf{u}$$ and define the sum of $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ as follows.

note.title: Definition of Vector Addition
note.heading: Definition of Vector Addition
note.paragraph: If $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ are vectors positioned so the initial point of $$\mathbf{v}$$ is at the terminal point of $$\mathbf{u}$$ , then the sum $$\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}$$ is the vector from the initial point of $$\mathbf{u}$$ to the terminal point of $$\mathbf{v}$$ .

section.paragraph: The definition of vector addition is illustrated in Figure 3. You can see why this definition is sometimes called the Triangle Law.

image.alt: Details Three vectors are displayed. The first vector, labeled vector u, slopes gradually upward to the right. The second vector, labeled vector v, begins from the tip of vector u and slopes steeply upward to the right. The third vector, labeled vector u + vector v, begins at the starting point of vector u and meets the tip of vector v.

section.paragraph: In Figure 4 we start with the same vectors $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ as in Figure 3 and draw another copy of $$\mathbf{v}$$ with the same initial point as $$\mathbf{u}$$ . Completing the parallelogram, we see that $$\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{u}$$ . This also gives another way to construct the sum: if we place $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ so they start at the same point, then $$\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}$$ lies along the diagonal of the parallelogram with $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ as sides. (This is called the Parallelogram Law.)

section.paragraph: We now define multiplication of a vector $$\mathbf{v}$$ by a real number $$c$$ . In this context we call the real number $$c$$ a scalar to distinguish it from a vector. For instance, we want the scalar multiple $$2\mathbf{v}$$ to be the same vector as the sum $$\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{v}$$ , which has the same direction as $$\mathbf{v}$$ but is twice as long. In general, we multiply a vector by a scalar as follows.

note.title: Definition of Scalar Multiplication
note.heading: Definition of Scalar Multiplication
note.paragraph: If $$c$$ is a scalar and $$\mathbf{v}$$ is a vector, then the scalar multiple $$c\mathbf{v}$$ is the vector whose length is $$|c|$$ times the length of $$\mathbf{v}$$ and whose direction is the same as $$\mathbf{v}$$ if $$c > 0$$ and is opposite to $$\mathbf{v}$$ if $$c < 0$$ . If $$c = 0$$ or $$\mathbf{v} = 0$$ , then $$c\mathbf{v} = 0$$ .

section.paragraph: This definition is illustrated in Figure 7. We see that real numbers work like scaling factors here; that’s why we call them scalars. Notice that two nonzero vectors are parallel if they are scalar multiples of one another. In particular, the vector $$- \mathbf{v} = ( - 1)\mathbf{v}$$ has the same length as $$\mathbf{v}$$ but points in the opposite direction. We call it the negative of $$\mathbf{v}$$ .

section.paragraph: By the difference $$\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}$$ of two vectors we mean
$$\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u} + \left( - \mathbf{v} \right)$$

For the vectors $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ shown in Figure 8(a), we can construct the difference $$\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}$$ by first drawing the negative of $$\mathbf{v}$$ , $$- \mathbf{v}$$ , and then adding it to $$\mathbf{u}$$ by the Parallelogram Law as in Figure 8(b). Alternatively, since $$\mathbf{v} + \left( {\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}} \right) = \mathbf{u}$$ , the vector $$\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}$$ , when added to $$\mathbf{v}$$ , gives $$\mathbf{u}$$ . So we could construct $$\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}$$ as in Figure 8(c) by means of the Triangle Law. Notice that if $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ both start from the same initial point, then $$\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}$$ connects the tip of $$\mathbf{v}$$ to the tip of $$\mathbf{u}$$ .

section.heading: Components of a Vector
section.paragraph: For some purposes it’s convenient to introduce a coordinate system that allows us to treat vectors algebraically. If we place the initial point of a vector $$\mathbf{a}$$ at the origin of a rectangular coordinate system, then the terminal point of $$\mathbf{a}$$ has coordinates of the form $$\left( {a_{1},a_{2}} \right)$$ or $$\left( {a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}} \right)$$ , depending on whether our coordinate system is two- or three-dimensional (see Figure 11). These coordinates are called the components of $$\mathbf{a}$$ and we write
$$\mathbf{a} = {\langle{a_{1},a_{2}}\rangle}$$
or
$$\mathbf{a} = {\langle{a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}}\rangle}$$

We use the notation $$\langle{a_{1},a_{2}}\rangle$$ for the ordered pair that refers to a vector so as not to confuse it with the ordered pair $$\left( {a_{1},a_{2}} \right)$$ that refers to a point in the plane.

section.paragraph: For instance, all of the vectors shown in Figure 12 are equivalent to the vector $$\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{OP}} = {\langle{3,2}\rangle}$$ whose terminal point is $$P\left( {3,2} \right)$$ . What they have in common is that the terminal point is reached from the initial point by a displacement of three units to the right and two upward. We can think of all these geometric vectors as representations of the algebraic vector $$\mathbf{a} = {\langle{3,2}\rangle}$$ . The particular representation $$\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{OP}}$$ from the origin to the point $$P\left( {3,2} \right)$$ is called the position vector of the point $$P$$ .

(See Figure 13.) Let’s consider any other representation of $$\mathbf{a}$$ by a directed line segment $$\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{AB}}$$ with initial point $$A\left( {x_{1},y_{1},z_{1}} \right)$$ and terminal point $$B\left( {x_{2},y_{2},z_{2}} \right)$$ . Then we must have $$x_{1} + a_{1} = x_{2}$$ , $$y_{1} + a_{2} = y_{2}$$ , and $$z_{1} + a_{3} = z_{2}$$ and so $$a_{1} = x_{2} - x_{1}$$ , $$a_{2} = y_{2} - y_{1}$$ , and $$a_{3} = z_{2} - z_{1}$$ . Thus we have the following result.

section.paragraph: The magnitude or length of the vector $$\mathbf{v}$$ is the length of any of its representations and is denoted by the symbol $$\left| \mathbf{v} \right|$$ or $$\left\| \mathbf{v} \right\|$$ . By using the distance formula to compute the length of a segment $$\mathit{OP}$$ , we obtain the following formulas.
The length of the two-dimensional vector $$\mathbf{a} = {\langle{a_{1},a_{2}}\rangle}$$ is
$$\left| \mathbf{a} \right| = \sqrt{a_{1}^{2} + a_{2}^{2}}$$

How do we add vectors algebraically? Figure 14 shows that if $$\mathbf{a} = {\langle{a_{1},a_{2}}\rangle}$$ and $$\mathbf{b} = {\langle{b_{1},b_{2}}\rangle}$$ , then their sum is $$\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b} = {\langle{a_{1} + b_{1},a_{2} + b_{2}}\rangle}$$ , at least for the case where the components are positive. In other words, to add algebraic vectors we add corresponding components. Similarly, to subtract vectors we subtract corresponding components. From the similar triangles in Figure 15 we see that the components of $$c\mathbf{a}$$ are $$ca_{1}$$ and $$ca_{2}$$ . So to multiply a vector by a scalar we multiply each component by that scalar.

Similarly, for three-dimensional vectors,

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: If $$\mathbf{a} = {\langle{4,0,3}\rangle}$$ and $$\mathbf{b} = {\langle{- 2,1,5}\rangle}$$ , find $$\left| \mathbf{a} \right|$$ and the vectors $$\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}$$ , $$\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{b}$$ , $$3\mathbf{b}$$ , and $$2\mathbf{a} + 5\mathbf{b}$$ .
Solution

$$\begin{array}{rcl} \left| \mathbf{a} \right| & = & {\sqrt{4^{2} + 0^{2} + 3^{2}} = \sqrt{25} = 5} \\ {\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}} & = & {{\langle{4,0,3}\rangle} + {\langle{- 2,1,5}\rangle}} \\ & = & {{\langle{4 + \left( {- 2} \right),0 + 1,3 + 5}\rangle} = {\langle{2,1,8}\rangle}} \\ {\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{b}} & = & {{\langle{4,0,3}\rangle} - {\langle{- 2,1,5}\rangle}} \\ & = & {{\langle{4 - \left( {- 2} \right),0 - 1,3 - 5}\rangle} = {\langle{6, - 1, - 2}\rangle}} \\ {3\mathbf{b}} & = & {3{\langle{- 2,1,5}\rangle} = {\langle{3\left( {- 2} \right),3(1),3(5)}\rangle} = {\langle{- 6,3,15}\rangle}} \\ {2\mathbf{a} + 5\mathbf{b}} & = & {2{\langle{4,0,3}\rangle} + 5{\langle{- 2,1,5}\rangle}} \\ & = & {{\langle{8,0,6}\rangle} + {\langle{- 10,5,25}\rangle} = {\langle{- 2,5,31}\rangle}} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: We denote by $$V_{2}$$ the set of all two-dimensional vectors and by $$V_{3}$$ the set of all three-dimensional vectors. More generally, we will later need to consider the set $$V_{n}$$ of all $$n$$ -dimensional vectors. An $$n$$ -dimensional vector is an ordered $$n$$ -tuple:
$$\mathbf{a} = {\langle{a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{n}}\rangle}$$

where $$a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{n}$$ are real numbers that are called the components of $$\mathbf{a}$$ . Addition and scalar multiplication in $$V_{n}$$ are defined in terms of components just as for the cases $$n = 2$$ and $$n = 3$$ .
Vectors in $$n$$ dimensions are used to list various quantities in an organized way. For instance, the components of a six-dimensional vector

might represent the prices of six different ingredients required to make a particular product. Four-dimensional vectors $$\langle{x,y,z,t}\rangle$$ are used in relativity theory, where the first three components specify a position in space and the fourth represents time.

section.paragraph: These eight properties of vectors can be readily verified either geometrically or algebraically. For instance, Property 1 can be seen from Figure 4 (it’s equivalent to the Parallelogram Law) or as follows for the case $$n = 2$$ :

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}} = {{\langle{a_{1},a_{2}}\rangle} + {\langle{b_{1},b_{2}}\rangle} = {\langle{a_{1} + b_{1},a_{2} + b_{2}}\rangle}}} \\ {\phantom{\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}} = {{\langle{b_{1} + a_{1},b_{2} + a_{2}}\rangle} = {\langle{b_{1},b_{2}}\rangle} + {\langle{a_{1},a_{2}}\rangle}}} \\ {\phantom{\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}} = {\mathbf{b} + \mathbf{a}}} \end{array}$$

We can see why Property 2 (the associative law) is true by looking at Figure 16 and applying the Triangle Law several times: the vector $$\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PQ}}$$ is obtained either by first constructing $$\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}$$ and then adding $$\mathbf{c}$$ or by adding $$\mathbf{a}$$ to the vector $$\mathbf{b} + \mathbf{c}$$ .

section.paragraph: Three vectors in $$V_{3}$$ play a special role. Let
$${\mathbf{i} = {\langle{1,0,0}\rangle}} {\mathbf{j} = {\langle{0,1,0}\rangle}} {\mathbf{k} = {\langle{0,0,1}\rangle}}$$

These vectors $$\mathbf{i}$$ , $$\mathbf{j}$$ , and $$\mathbf{k}$$ are called the standard basis vectors. They have length $$1$$ and point in the directions of the positive $$x$$ -, $$y$$ -, and $$z$$ -axes. Similarly, in two dimensions we define $$\mathbf{i} = {\langle{1,0}\rangle}$$ and $$\mathbf{j} = {\langle{0,1}\rangle}$$ . (See Figure 17.)

section.paragraph: If $$\mathbf{a} = {\langle{a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}}\rangle}$$ , then we can write

$$\begin{array}{lcl} \mathbf{a} & = & {{\langle{a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}}\rangle} = {\langle{a_{1},0,0}\rangle} + {\langle{0,a_{2},0}\rangle} + {\langle{0,0,a_{3}}\rangle}} \\ & = & {a_{1}{\langle{1,0,0}\rangle} + a_{2}{\langle{0,1,0}\rangle} + a_{3}{\langle{0,0,1}\rangle}} \end{array}$$
$$\mathbf{a} = {a_{1}\mathbf{i} + a_{2}\mathbf{j} + a_{3}\mathbf{k}}$$
Thus any vector in $$V_{3}$$ can be expressed in terms of $$\mathbf{i}$$ , $$\mathbf{j}$$ , and $$\mathbf{k}$$ . For instance,
$${\langle{1, - 2,6}\rangle} = \mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j} + 6\mathbf{k}$$
Similarly, in two dimensions, we can write
$$\mathbf{a} = {\langle{a_{1},a_{2}}\rangle} = a_{1}\mathbf{i} + a_{2}\mathbf{j}$$

The second vector, labeled a_1 vector i, begins at the origin and runs along the positive x axis until directly below the point (a_1, a_2). From the tip of the second vector, the third vector, labeled a_2 vector j, rises vertically upward and meets the tip of vector a at (a_1, a_2). Four vectors are graphed in the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The first vector labeled vector a, begins at the origin and slopes upward into the first octant until a point (a_1, a_2, a_3). The second vector, labeled a_1 vector i, begins at the origin and runs along the positive x axis. From the tip of the second vector, the third vector, labeled a_2 vector j, runs parallel to the positive y axis until directly below the point (a_1, a_2, a_3). The fourth vector, labeled a_3 vector k, rise vertically upward and meets the tip of vector a at (a_1, a_2, a_3).

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: If $$\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j} - 3\mathbf{k}$$ and $$\mathbf{b} = 4\mathbf{i} + 7\mathbf{k}$$ , express the vector $$2\mathbf{a} + 3\mathbf{b}$$ in terms of $$\mathbf{i}$$ , $$\mathbf{j}$$ , and $$\mathbf{k}$$ .
Solution Using Properties 1, 2, 5, 6, and 7 of vectors, we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {{2\mathbf{a} + 3\mathbf{b}} = {2\left( {\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j} - 3\mathbf{k}} \right) + 3\left( {4\mathbf{i} + 7\mathbf{k}} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{2\mathbf{a} + 3\mathbf{b}} = {2\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j} - 6\mathbf{k} + 12\mathbf{i} + 21\mathbf{k} = 14\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j} + 15\mathbf{k}}} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: A unit vector is a vector whose length is $$1$$ . For instance, $$\mathbf{i}$$ , $$\mathbf{j}$$ , and $$\mathbf{k}$$ are all unit vectors. In general, if $$\mathbf{a} \neq 0$$ , then the unit vector that has the same direction as $$\mathbf{a}$$ is
$$\mathbf{u} = \frac{1}{\left| \mathbf{a} \right|}\mathbf{a} = \frac{\mathbf{a}}{\left| \mathbf{a} \right|}$$

In order to verify this, we let $$c = 1 \slash \left| \mathbf{a} \right|$$ . Then $$\mathbf{u} = c\mathbf{a}$$ and $$c$$ is a positive scalar, so $$\mathbf{u}$$ has the same direction as $$\mathbf{a}$$ . Also
$$\left| \mathbf{u} \right| = \left| {c\mathbf{a}} \right| = |c|\left| \mathbf{a} \right| = \frac{1}{\left| \mathbf{a} \right|}\left| \mathbf{a} \right| = 1$$

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Find the unit vector in the direction of the vector $$2\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} - 2\mathbf{k}$$ .
Solution The given vector has length
$$\left| {2\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} - 2\mathbf{k}} \right| = \sqrt{2^{2} + \left( {- 1} \right)^{2} + \left( {- 2} \right)^{2}} = \sqrt{9} = 3$$
so, by Equation 4, the unit vector with the same direction is
$$\frac{1}{3}\left( {2\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} - 2\mathbf{k}} \right) = \frac{2}{3}\mathbf{i} - \frac{1}{3}\mathbf{j} - \frac{2}{3}\mathbf{k}$$

section.heading: Applications
section.paragraph: Vectors are useful in many aspects of physics and engineering. In Chapter 13 we will see how they describe the velocity and acceleration of objects moving in space. Here we first look at forces.

A force is represented by a vector because it has both magnitude (measured in pounds or newtons) and direction. If several forces are acting on an object, the resultant force experienced by the object is the vector sum of these forces.

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: A $$100$$ -lb weight hangs from two wires as shown in Figure 19. Find the tensions (forces) $$\mathbf{T}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{T}_{2}$$ in the wires and the magnitudes of these tensions.

image.alt: Details The figure is a two dimensional illustration of a weight hung from horizontal support by two wires and two vectors. The first wire is attached to the left of the support and slopes downward to the right at an angle of 50 degrees from the support. The second rope is attached to the right of the support and slopes gradually downwards to the left at an angle of 32 degrees from the support and meets the first rope. The weight is hung from this common point and is labeled 100. From the weight, a vector labeled vector T_1 runs along the rope pointing up and to the left toward the support. From the weight, another vector labeled vector T_2 runs along the rope pointing up and to the right toward the support.

example.paragraph: Solution We first express $$\mathbf{T}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{T}_{2}$$ in terms of their horizontal and vertical components. From Figure 20 we see that
$$\mathbf{T}_{1} = - \left| \mathbf{T}_{1} \right|\cos 50^{{^\circ}}\mathbf{i} + \left| \mathbf{T}_{1} \right|\sin 50^{{^\circ}}\mathbf{j}$$
$$\mathbf{T}_{2} = \left| \mathbf{T}_{2} \right|\cos 32^{{^\circ}}\mathbf{i} + \left| \mathbf{T}_{2} \right|\sin 32^{{^\circ}}\mathbf{j}$$

image.alt: Details The figure shows an illustration of a triangle and seven vectors. The triangle has a horizontal top side. The left side is at an angle of 50 degrees from the horizontal side. The right side is at an angle of 32 degrees from the horizontal top side. From the bottom vertex of the triangle, a vector labeled vector T_1, runs along the left side of the triangle. From the bottom vertex, a horizontal vector extends leftward making an angle of 50 degrees with vector T_1. From the tip of the horizontal vector, a vertical vector rises upward to meet the tip of vector T_1. From the bottom vertex of the triangle, a vector labeled vector T_2, runs along the right side of the triangle. From the bottom vertex, a horizontal vector extends rightward making an angle of 32 degrees with vector T_2. From the tip of the horizontal vector, a vertical vector rises upward to meet the tip of vector T_2. From the bottom vertex, a vector descends vertically downward and is labeled vector w.

example.paragraph: The resultant $$\mathbf{T}_{1} + \mathbf{T}_{2}$$ of the tensions counterbalances the weight $$\mathbf{w} = - 100\mathbf{j}$$ and so we must have
$$\mathbf{T}_{1} + \mathbf{T}_{2} = - \mathbf{w} = 100\mathbf{j}$$
Thus

$$\left( {- \left| \mathbf{T}_{1} \right|\cos 50^{{^\circ}} + \left| \mathbf{T}_{2} \right|\cos 32^{{^\circ}}} \right)\mathbf{i} + \left( {\left| \mathbf{T}_{1} \right|\sin 50^{{^\circ}} + \left| \mathbf{T}_{2} \right|\sin 32^{{^\circ}}} \right)\mathbf{j} = 100\mathbf{j}$$
Equating components, we get

$$\begin{array}{ccl} {- \left| \mathbf{T}_{1} \right|\cos 50^{{^\circ}} + \left| \mathbf{T}_{2} \right|\cos 32^{{^\circ}}} & = & 0 \\ {\left| \mathbf{T}_{1} \right|\sin 50^{{^\circ}} + \left| \mathbf{T}_{2} \right|\sin 32^{{^\circ}}} & = & 100 \end{array}$$
Solving the first of these equations for $$\left| \mathbf{T}_{2} \right|$$ and substituting into the second, we get

$$\begin{array}{ccl} {\left| \mathbf{T}_{1} \right|\sin 50^{{^\circ}} + \frac{\left| \mathbf{T}_{1} \right|\cos 50^{{^\circ}}}{\cos 32^{{^\circ}}}\sin 32^{{^\circ}}} & = & 100 \\ {\left| \mathbf{T}_{1} \right|\left( {\sin 50^{{^\circ}} + \cos 50^{{^\circ}}\frac{\sin 32^{{^\circ}}}{\cos 32^{{^\circ}}}} \right)} & = & 100 \end{array}$$
So the magnitudes of the tensions are
$$\left| \mathbf{T}_{1} \right| = \frac{100}{\sin 50^{{^\circ}} + \tan 32^{{^\circ}}\cos 50^{{^\circ}}} \approx 85.64{lb}$$
and
$$\left| \mathbf{T}_{2} \right| = \frac{\left| \mathbf{T}_{1} \right|\cos 50^{{^\circ}}}{\cos 32^{{^\circ}}} \approx 64.91{lb}$$
Substituting these values in (5) and (6), we obtain the tension vectors
$$\begin{array}{cll} \mathbf{T}_{1} & \approx & {- 55.05\mathbf{i} + 65.60\mathbf{j}} \\ \mathbf{T}_{2} & \approx & {55.05\mathbf{i} + 34.40\mathbf{j}} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: If an airplane is flying in wind, then the true course, or track, of the plane is the direction of the resultant of the velocity vectors of the plane and of the wind. The ground speed of the plane is the magnitude of the resultant. Similarly, a boat navigating through flowing water follows a true course in the direction of the resultant of the velocity vectors of the boat and of the water current.

example.heading: Example 8
example.paragraph: A woman launches a boat from the south shore of a straight river that flows directly west at $$4{mi}/h$$ . She wants to land at the point directly across on the opposite shore. If the speed of the boat (relative to the water) is $$8{mi}/h$$ , in what direction should she steer the boat in order to arrive at the desired landing point?

Solution Let’s choose coordinate axes with the origin at the initial position of the boat, as shown in Figure 21. The velocity of the river current is $$\mathbf{v}_{c} = - 4\mathbf{i}$$ and, since the speed of the boat (in still water) is $$8{mi}/h$$ , the boat’s velocity is $$\mathbf{v}_{b} = 8\left( \cos\theta\mathbf{i} + \sin\theta\mathbf{j} \right)$$ , where $$\theta$$ is as shown in the figure. The resultant velocity is

$$\begin{array}{l} {\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}_{b} + \mathbf{v}_{c}} \\ {\phantom{\mathbf{v}} = 8\cos\theta\mathbf{i} + 8\sin\theta\mathbf{j} - 4\mathbf{i} = \left( - 4 + 8\cos\theta \right)\mathbf{i} + \left( 8\sin\theta \right)\mathbf{j}} \end{array}$$
We want the true course of the boat to be directly north, so the $$x$$ -component of $$\mathbf{v}$$ must be zero:
$$\left. - 4 + 8\cos\theta = 0 \Rightarrow \cos\theta = \frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \theta = 60^{{^\circ}} \right.$$
Thus the woman should steer the boat in the direction $$\theta = 60^{{^\circ}}$$ , or $$N30^{{^\circ}}E$$ .

image.alt: Details The x y coordinate plane is superimposed on a two-dimensional rendering of an overhead view of a boat on the water. The boat is in the first quadrant, with the back of the boat at the origin and the tip of the boat pointing up and to the right. A compass rose is placed at the top left corner with the North parallel to the positive y axis. Three vectors are drawn on the x y coordinate space. The first vector, labeled vector v_b, is along with the boat, and slopes upward to the right at an angle theta from the positive x axis. The second vector, labeled vector v, is along the positive y axis and points vertically upward. The third vector, labeled vector v_c, is along the negative x axis and points horizontally rightward.

example.paragraph: When describing directions for navigation, we often use a bearing, such as $$N20^{{^\circ}}W$$ , which means from the northerly direction, turn $$20^{{^\circ}}$$ toward west. (Note that a bearing always begins with either north or south.)

section.heading: Discovery Project The Shape of a Hanging Chain
section.paragraph: In Section 3.11 we stated that a heavy flexible chain or cable suspended between two points at the same height takes the shape of a curve called a catenary (a term reportedly coined by Thomas Jefferson) with equation $$y = a\cosh(x/a)$$ . Here we use the interpretation of the derivative as the slope of a tangent to derive this equation.

Suppose that a chain (or cable) of uniform linear mass density $$\rho$$ is hanging between two points, as shown in the figure. We place the origin at the vertex of the catenary, and let $$(x,y)$$ be any point on the curve, $$x > 0$$ . (By symmetry, if $$x < 0$$ we obtain a similar result.)

image.alt: Details The figure has two parts. In the first part, a horizontal bar with a cable hanging from it and three vectors are drawn on the x y coordinate plane. The horizontal bar is drawn above the x axis, running parallel to it. The cable is attached to two points on the bar such that it traces a parabola in the x y plane with its vertex at the origin. The first vector, labeled vector T_0, begins at the origin, and runs horizontally leftward, along the negative x axis. The second vector, labeled vector w, begins at a point on the cable, up and to the right of the origin, and descends vertically downward. The third vector, labeled vector T, begins at a point labeled (x, y), on the cable in the first quadrant and slopes upward to the right, tangent to the cable at (x, y). The second part of the figure displayed a right triangle composed of three vectors. The triangle has a horizontal top side labeled vector T_0, pointing leftward, a vertical side on the left, labeled vector w, pointing downward, and a hypotenuse that slopes upward to the right, labeled vector T, pointing up and to the right.

section.paragraph: Consider the section of the chain from the origin to $$(x,y)$$ . The forces that act on the section are the downward gravitational force $$\mathbf{w}$$ and the tensions $$\mathbf{T}_{0}$$ and $$\mathbf{T}$$ at each end of the section—each of which is tangent to the curve. Because the section of chain is in equilibrium, we know that
$$\mathbf{T}_{0} + \mathbf{T} + \mathbf{w} = 0$$

list.item: Let $$y = f(x)$$ be the equation of the curve and let $$s(x)$$ be the arc length function (Equation 8.1.5) from the origin to the point $$(x,y)$$ . Show that $$\left. \mathbf{T} = \langle \middle| \mathbf{T}_{0} \middle| ,g\rho s(x)\rangle \right.$$ where $$g$$ is the acceleration due to gravity.

By interpreting $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dx}$$ as the slope of a tangent at $$(x,y)$$ , show that $$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = \frac{s(x)}{a}$$ where $$\left. a = \middle| \mathbf{T}_{0} \middle| /g\rho \right.$$ , a constant.

Differentiate both sides of the differential equation in Problem 2 and use Equation 8.1.6 to obtain the second-order differential equation $$\frac{d^{2}y}{\mathit{dx}^{2}} = \frac{1}{a}\sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} \right)^{2}}$$ with initial conditions $$y(0) = 0$$ (the curve passes through the origin) and $$y^{\prime}(0) = 0$$ (the tangent at the origin is horizontal). Solve this equation by first substituting $$z = \mathit{dy}/\mathit{dx}$$ and then solving the resulting first-order differential equation. Conclude that the equation of the curve is $$y = a\cosh\frac{x}{a} - a$$
Graph $$y = a\cosh(x/a) - a$$ for $$a = \frac{1}{2}$$ , $$a = 1$$ , and $$a = 3$$ . How does the value of $$a$$ affect the shape of the curve?
